label: Size and power of a test — mastery test (unseen)

items.stem: The size of a test is the probability that it:
options: rejects H₀ when H₀ is true
rejects H₀ when H₁ is true
fails to reject H₀ when H₁ is true
fails to reject H₀ when H₀ is true
items.explanation: The size is the Type I error rate, α = P(reject H₀ | H₀ true). Option B is the power, option C is the Type II error, and option D is the correct non-rejection, 1 − α.

items.stem: If β denotes the probability of a Type II error, the power of the test is:
items.explanation: Power is the probability of rejecting a false null, which is one minus the probability of failing to do so: 1 − β. Note that some textbooks write β(θ) for the power function itself, in which case power = β(θ) — always read the stem for the convention in use.

items.stem: The power function π(θ) of a test, evaluated at the null value θ₀, equals:
items.explanation: π(θ₀) = P(reject H₀ | θ₀) is exactly the definition of the size. This identity is the quickest check on any power function you derive: substitute θ₀ and α must come back.

items.stem: A rejection region and two parameter values are given. Arrange the steps of computing the size and the power in the correct order.
items.explanation: Write the region out as a set of values first — this is where 'more than 3' is distinguished from 'at least 3'. Then the null value gives the size, then the alternative gives the power, and the sanity check that power exceeds size comes last. This is the pattern of June 2026 Q43.
items: A. Evaluate the probability of the region under the null value
B. Evaluate the probability of the same region under the alternative value
C. Write the rejection region explicitly as a set of values of the statistic
D. Check that the power exceeds the size

items.stem: Which change raises the power of a test without raising its size?
options: using a two-sided alternative instead of a one-sided one
widening the rejection region at fixed n
items.explanation: Only more data improves the detection rate at no cost in false alarms. Raising α, or equivalently widening the region, raises power and the false-alarm rate together. Going two-sided lowers power against a one-sided departure, because the cut-off moves out from 1.645 to 1.96.

items.stem: A test of H₀ based on discrete data has rejection probability 0.031 under the null. Which description is correct?
options: it is a level-0.05 test of size 0.031
it is invalid, since the size must equal the stated level
items.explanation: The size is the exact null rejection probability, 0.031; the level is any upper bound on it, so 0.05 is a valid level. For discrete statistics only finitely many sizes are attainable and an exact 0.05 usually is not one of them, so this is the ordinary honest description, not a defect.

items.stem: A coin is tossed 5 times to test H₀: p = 1/2 against H₁: p = 3/4, and H₀ is rejected if more than 3 heads are obtained. The size of the test is:
items.explanation: More than 3 heads means X = 4 or 5. Under p = 1/2, P(X ≥ 4) = [C(5,4) + C(5,5)]/32 = 6/32 = 0.1875. Option B is P(X ≥ 3), the answer to 'at least 3'; option C is P(X = 5) alone; option D is P(X = 4) alone.
items.check: The size uses p = 1/2 and the values 4 and 5 only. If the number 3 entered the count, the inequality in the stem was read as 'at least'.

items.stem: For the same test — 5 tosses, reject H₀: p = 1/2 if more than 3 heads appear — the power against H₁: p = 3/4 is:
items.explanation: P(X ≥ 4 | p = 3/4) = C(5,4)(3/4)⁴(1/4) + (3/4)⁵ = 405/1024 + 243/1024 = 648/1024 = 0.6328. Option A is P(X = 4) alone, option B is P(X = 5) alone, and option D is the size — computed under the null instead of the alternative. This is June 2026 Q49.
items.check: The power must use p = 3/4 and must exceed the size 0.1875. An answer equal to 0.1875 means the null value was substituted.

items.stem: The density is f(x; θ) = 1/θ for 0 ≤ x ≤ θ. To test H₀: θ = 1 against H₁: θ = 2 from a single observation, the critical region is x ≥ 0.5. The power of the test is:
items.explanation: Under θ = 2 the density is 1/2 on the interval 0 to 2, so P(X ≥ 0.5) = 1.5 × (1/2) = 0.75. Option A is the size, computed under θ = 1, which is the error the options are built around. This is June 2026 Q39.
items.check: The power uses θ = 2, so the rectangle has width 2 and height 1/2. If the width used was 1, the null value was substituted.

items.stem: X₁,…,X₂₅ are iid N(μ, 100) with σ = 10 known. H₀: μ = 50 is tested against H₁: μ > 50 at α = 0.05, rejecting when x̄ > 50 + 1.645(σ/√n). The power at μ = 54 is approximately:
items.explanation: σ/√n = 10/5 = 2, so the region is x̄ > 50 + 1.645(2) = 53.29. Under μ = 54 this gives P(Z > (53.29 − 54)/2) = P(Z > −0.355) = 0.6387. Equivalently π(54) = P(Z > 1.645 − (54 − 50)√25/10) = P(Z > 1.645 − 2). Option B is the Type II error 1 − 0.6387, and option C is the size — the power read under the null instead of the alternative.
items.check: Use π(μ) = P(Z > z_α − (μ − μ₀)√n/σ). Here (54 − 50)(5)/10 = 2, so the argument is 1.645 − 2 = −0.355.

items.stem: For a one-sided test of the composite null H₀: μ ≤ 100 that rejects for large x̄, the size of the test is computed at:
options: any convenient value inside the null, since all give the same answer
the value of μ under the alternative
μ = 100, the boundary of the null
items.explanation: The size of a test with a composite null is the supremum of the power function over the null range. Here the power function increases in μ, so over μ ≤ 100 its largest value sits at the boundary μ = 100. Interior values give smaller rejection probabilities and so understate the size.

items.stem: Consider the size and power of a test. Read the four statements and decide which are correct.
items.explanation: A is true, straight from the definitions. B is false — the power is computed under the alternative, which is the commonest error in the topic. C is true: the power function passes through the size at the null value. D is false — a test can have correct size and no power at all, as the test that ignores the data and rejects with probability α shows.
statements: The significance level α is chosen by the experimenter before the data are seen.
The power of a test is computed under the null hypothesis.
The power function evaluated at the null value equals the size.
A test with the correct size necessarily has acceptable power.

A.why: True. The experimenter chooses the target level α in advance; the actual size is then determined by the rejection rule and can be smaller than α, especially for discrete tests.

B.why: False. The power is the rejection probability under the alternative — or at whatever parameter value is named. Only the size uses the null.

C.why: True. π(θ₀) = P(reject | θ₀) = α by definition, which makes it a useful check on a derived power function.

D.why: False. Controlling the size alone guarantees nothing: a test that rejects with probability α regardless of the data has exact size α and power α everywhere.

items.stem: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid N(μ, 25). Test H₀: μ = 100 against H₁: μ > 100 at α = 0.05. The smallest n for which the power at μ = 102 is at least 0.90 is (use z₀.₀₅ = 1.645, z₀.₁₀ = 1.282):
items.explanation: √n ≥ (1.645 + 1.282)(5)/2 = 2.927(2.5) = 7.3175, so n ≥ 53.54 and the smallest integer is 54. Option B rounds to the nearest integer instead of up, leaving the power just under at 0.897. Option A uses the difference 1.645 − 1.282 rather than the sum.
items.check: The two normal points ADD. If 2.927 does not appear in your working, the signs are wrong; and the final answer is rounded up, never to nearest.

items.stem: At α = 0.05, the two-sided test of H₀: μ = μ₀ based on x̄ with σ known rejects when:
items.explanation: A two-sided alternative splits α across both tails, 0.025 in each, so the multiplier is 1.96. Option C puts the whole 5% in each tail, giving a size of 0.10. Options A and D are one-sided regions, and D also uses the two-sided multiplier on a one-sided region, giving size 0.025.

items.stem: Two tests of the same H₀: μ = μ₀ use the same data and the same α = 0.05: one is one-sided against μ > μ₀, the other two-sided. At a particular alternative μ₁ > μ₀:
options: both have the same power, since α is the same
the two-sided test has the greater power
the one-sided test has the greater power
items.explanation: The one-sided test spends its whole 5% on the relevant side, so its cut-off is at 1.645 standard errors instead of 1.96 and it rejects more readily against a departure in that direction. The two-sided test pays for its ability to detect departures either way. The ordering holds for every σ and every n.

items.stem: In the one-sided normal test with σ known, the power at a fixed alternative increases with:
items.explanation: The power is P(Z > z_α − (μ − μ₀)√n/σ), and n enters only as √n. This is why quadrupling the sample size halves the gap detectable at a given power, and why sample-size answers are larger than intuition suggests.

items.stem: A test of H₀: p = 1/2 based on 5 tosses rejects for large X. Consider the following statements about attaining an exact size of 0.05.
items.explanation: A is false: the attainable sizes are the tail probabilities 1/32 = 0.031, 6/32 = 0.1875 and so on, and 0.05 is not among them. B is true — the randomised test rejects at X = 5 and with probability γ at X = 4, with γ = (0.05 − 0.03125)/(5/32) = 0.12. C is true. D is false: with size reduced from 0.1875 to 0.05, the power falls to 0.2848, well below 0.6328.
statements: A non-randomised test based on X can attain size exactly 0.05.
A randomised test attains size exactly 0.05 by rejecting with probability 0.12 when X = 4.
Reporting the test as 'level 0.05, size 0.031' is a valid description of the non-randomised test.
The randomised size-0.05 test has higher power at p = 3/4 than the non-randomised test that rejects when X ≥ 4.

A.why: False. X takes six values, so only six tail probabilities are available: 0.031, 0.1875, 0.5 and so on. None equals 0.05.

C.why: True, and it is the description a practising statistician would use, since the level is an upper bound on the size.

D.why: False. The non-randomised X ≥ 4 test has size 0.1875 and power 0.6328; cutting the size to 0.05 cuts the power to 0.2848. Lower false-alarm rate always costs power at fixed n.

items.stem: X₁,…,X₁₆ are iid N(μ, 16). The two-sided test of H₀: μ = 10 at α = 0.05 rejects when |x̄ − 10| > 1.96. The power at μ = 12, to four decimal places, is:
items.explanation: σ/√n = 4/4 = 1, so the region is x̄ > 11.96 or x̄ < 8.04. Under μ = 12: P(Z > −0.04) = 0.5160 and P(Z < −3.96) = 0.00004, summing to 0.5160. Option D is the one-sided test's power at the same alternative, which is higher because its cut-off is 1.645 rather than 1.96.
items.check: A two-sided power is a sum over both tails. The far tail is tiny but not zero, and the total must come out below the one-sided power 0.6387.

items.stem: A test is described as unbiased. This means:
options: its power function is symmetric about θ₀
the statistic it uses is an unbiased estimator of θ
its size equals its stated level exactly
its power at every alternative is at least its size
items.explanation: An unbiased test satisfies π(θ) ≥ α for every θ in the alternative — it never rejects a false null less often than it rejects a true one. The word is unrelated to unbiased estimation, which is option B's confusion, and it says nothing about attaining the level exactly or about symmetry.

items.stem: The power function of a test of H₀: μ = 10 is drawn and has a minimum value of 0.05 at μ = 10, rising towards 1 in both directions. The test is:
options: a biased test, since the power dips
items.explanation: Rising in both directions is the signature of a two-sided rejection region, and the minimum value of a power function at the null value is the size, so α = 0.05. It is not biased: the power is at least 0.05 at every alternative, with equality only at the null value itself, which is not in the alternative.
